title: What is the purpose of software
text:
What is the purpose of software

Practical and existential questions for IT Design and Development.

I first asked myself this question for a bit of a laugh. This was at the dawn of 2023, during the rise of the LLM. Doomsayers and prophets alike said AI will allow us to produce so much more, so much more quickly.

But I had to ask… so much more of what, and to what end? The answer is not superficial.

This question has been at times haunting and at times obsessing me for years. Now that software can use software for us, what exactly was the point of us using it in the first place? AI will be a force multiplier, undoubtedly, but what is it multiplying? What is software for and what will it mean for the world when we have exponentially more of it?

Here’s the first clue: producing does not equal productivity, not in the technical sense.

I had a deeply unsettling hunch and needed to piece together my thoughts before I could share it. I traveled from slushy Danish winters to the equatorial highlands of Kenya, from humid-AF Tokyo to ever-so-sunny Spain — no, not to look for answers, that was just part of a fairly generic midlife crisis — and three years appears to have been the gestation period for this theory. Now that some early evidence supports the theory, I’m compelled to complete it, imperfectly but as well as I can.

You’re not going to like the conclusions. I have little in here for the AI optimists nor for the anti-AI anarchists, and not much to please anyone in between. The best I can hope for is that you’ll read my questions and hypotheses and vehemently disagree… and that you’ll have a theory why you disagree.

I’ll come back to this in the end, if there’s one exegesis to take from this text, it’s a plea to use your own mind.

Software has not made us more productive

I’ve been accused, fairly, of taking the long and winding road in stating my thesis, a Shyamalan-esque approach to nonfiction. (Exhibit A: the first 300 words of this article). Ok, that’s my apology and now I’ll get to the point.

So what is the purpose of software? The two words that leap to mind are efficiency and productivity. Or, efficiency that leads to productivity. This was my initial thought; it’s nearly everyone’s initial thought. It’s so often repeated that we take it for granted.

Yet, the facts of our economic growth prove this is not true.

Here’s how my internal dialogue went:

Limbic system chorus, all together now: “The purpose of software is to make us more productive.”
Prefrontal cortex: “But does it?”
Amygdala: “Of course it does!”
Prefrontal cortex: “No, I don’t think it does, actually.”

We can condense the ensuing three years of internal debate into this handy table of contents (spoilerish, skip ahead if you really like Shyamalan):

The Naivety → The Function → The Origins → The Evolution → The Law → The Reckoning

Part 1 — Software has not made us more productive, aka The Naivety

While computing power has increased 1 trillion times (10¹²) since 1971, productivity growth has declined to less than half of mid-1900s levels.

Part 2 — The Function, The role of software in society

The purpose of software is not to increase productivity but to increase the density of information in any unit of digital output.

Part 3 — The Origins, A brief history of software

A look at both a history of the inventions and a history of the applications, and the causal links between the two.

Part 4 — The Evolution, How markets mimic biology

Differentiating between teleonomy vs. teleology: Natural ecosystems explain the past, present, and future.

Part 5 — The Law, The physics of dissipative structures

Software — like a whirlpool, a flame, or a living cell — survives only through continuous energy consumption, and collapses the moment the flow stops.

Part 6 — The Reckoning, How the World Will Adapt to AI

AI will not change the purpose of software or its relationship with productivity. AI will be a General Purpose Technology in every sense but purpose… Yet, this time it is different.

The logic of each point follows the previous. First we need to convince you that productivity gains from software are a myth.

This fear (should we call it a fear? Maybe queasiness) surfaced nearly 40 years ago. The economist and Nobel Laureate Robert Solow wrote, “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.”

That was 1987. A decade later productivity growth was increasing; economists and technologists breathed a sigh of relief. There’s often a “productivity lag” between the invention of a disruptive technology and its effective use. Surely this was why it took a few decades for growth to materialize?

Alas, though the brief burst of the late 90s brought us nearly to previous levels of growth, it fizzled out just as quickly. We’re now back to flirting with century lows of productivity growth.

Let’s look at the data to debunk our collective misconception.

Productivity in the Age of Information

Paul Krugman, another Nobel winner, wrote in his NYT column in March 2023, “Like previous leaps in technology, [AI] will make the economy more productive.” He also concluded that, thanks to LLMs, “the longer-run prospects for economic growth do look better now.”

Krugman seems to be a proponent of the productivity lag theory. Still, he gently cautioned restraint in projecting any rapid acceleration of economic growth.

The title of that column sums it up, A.I. May Change Everything, but Probably Not Too Quickly. He suggested that “ChatGPT and whatever follows are probably an economic story for the 2030s, not for the next few years.”

To support his points, he presented a chart of productivity growth over the last 120 years. This chart measures the annual rate of non-farm labor productivity growth over the previous 10 years.

Labor productivity growth from 1920–1970, aside from the Great Depression, was mostly well above 2%. Since the invention of the microprocessor in 1971 it has been mostly below 2%.

The annotations on the chart are Krugman’s. In his words, “for at least two decades after Moore’s Law kicked in, America, far from experiencing a productivity boom, suffered from a protracted productivity slowdown.”

The long post-WWII boom marked with a “?” is suggested to be the result of an “age of continuity” during which we got better at using technologies that had been around for a while, like the internal combustion engine.

The economist Robert J. Gordon identified five “Great Inventions” from 1870 to 1970: electricity, urban sanitation, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, the internal combustion engine, and modern communication. He proposed that this 100 years of transformational General Purpose Technologies (GPTs — no relation to ChatGPT) was a one-off phase, never to return.

Krugman leans techno-optimist, but despite his compliment sandwich approach, some folks got mad at Paul for his column. (That seems to be what happens when you present an opinion with a logical argument.) They didn’t like that he questioned the productivity gains of IT, even with a semi-favorable conclusion.

But then again, you can’t blame them. When you ask questions — questions about someone’s raison d’être (I believe that’s French for “raisin of existence”), it really shrivels some grapes.

People put a lot of stock in the work they do. We all do. When I do the math to estimate I’ve spent forty thousand hours professionally engaged with technology — a quarter of my 4,000 weeks on this blue dot — asking why can get a bit uncomfortable.

So Krugman was compelled to write a follow up, The Internet Was an Economic Disappointment, to present more data to the gnostics.

The Information Age has been an economic disappointment

I’m taking things a step further than Krugman. We can rely on the same foundational data, though.

In his follow up piece, he looked at data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics on labor productivity and Total Factor Productivity. Total Factor Productivity, incidentally, is a measure created by our pal Solow. It includes the impact of capital and worker knowledge as well as hours of labor; it’s a preferred way to measure the effect of technological progress.

As Krugman explains, “A truly fundamental technological innovation should cause sustained growth in both these measures, especially total factor productivity.” In the chart below he switches to a forward looking measurement, growth over the 25 years following the dates on the chart. This way we can attempt to identify inflection points and their causes.

We’ve got one bump that lines up with the end of the dot com “boom” 25 years later. Other than that, the Information Age looks pretty flat.

To be ultra-explicit here and avoid fights I’m not looking for (there are plenty I am looking for), what we’re talking about is a deceleration of productivity growth, not the absence of growth.

But why stop there, has software helped any other macro KPIs?

This chart is a plot of the ratio of the S&P 500 to GDP, which conveniently ignores inflation. While it’s not apples-to-apples — stock prices bundle profits, expectations, and multiples — the direction is what counts. S&P 500 growth is three and a half times the overall economy since those measurements began; all of that advantage and then some accumulated since 1980. Corporate profits’ share of GDP has roughly doubled since the 1980s, and those profits have concentrated in the largest firms. The market is pricing what we’ll attempt to explain in Part 4 on the competitive benefits of information technology.

Software may have helped the big guys get bigger but it has not made us more productive.

Macro nits to pick

In case you’re already seething, let me take a moment to assure you that I’m not anti-technology. I use software and AI all day every day. I don’t propose that we throw away our phones and go live in a commune. I’m as excited as the next person about what new wonders we’ll create.

I’m just trying to get to the bottom of what technology is doing for us — or to us — in aggregate.

I enjoy technology, you enjoy technology — surely this is an intangible benefit we should consider. Has quality of life increased since the semiconductor was invented? We have Spotify, Netflix, LLMs, and very large TVs. Still, for the previous century we had vinyl, cinemas, Encyclopedia Britannica, and… cinemas.

It’s hard to argue that indoor plumbing, medical sanitation, and washing machines didn’t cause a greater increase in quality of life.

In an effort to leave no stone unturned, I jotted a list of possible “purposes” of software:

  • Do things quicker, easier
  • Remove physical things
  • New capabilities that we couldn’t do before
  • Level the playing field of ability
  • Surface information that would otherwise be difficult to find and coordinate
  • Solving problems?
  • Improved analytics/mathematical capabilities
  • Entertainment & games (potentially a counterweight to productivity… look at hours worked)
  • Digitizing the analog — preventing data loss

All of these avenues led to dead ends. Not just dead ends but depressing one-line obituaries. “He was an honest man, and well liked by his peers.”

Any of the above can be considered benefits, but none an end in and of themselves. Much of it can be distilled to an abstraction of data and a facility for the average person to corral that data. We’ll come back to this.

You may have seen my note to self in the list above. I needed to consider productivity per person, or even per hour.

Here’s a log chart of real (inflation adjusted) gross domestic product per person in the US.

Is it slightly concave, or is it slightly convex?

How about hours worked?

From the early 1950s at more than 2,000 hours, we reduced annual working hours to 1,771 by 1982. Relative to that year, things have stayed fairly consistent:

Year — Hours — % relative to 1982

  • 2000 — 1,845 — 104.2%
  • 2009 — 1,730 — 97.7%
  • 2017 — 1,757 — 99.2%
  • 2021 — 1,820 — 102.8%

Anecdotally, I have to put an asterisk next to the hours-worked* data. In the mid-90s (incidentally, the growth years) and prior, when knowledge workers left work they were done with work. Previous generations clocked out. Now information workers are generally expected to be on call every waking hour.

I would be hard pressed to find anyone working in IT today who doesn’t reopen their laptop after dinner to wrap up some work. Virtually every hour we feel compelled to keep an eye on work email and, god help us, Slack.

On a true per capita, per hour basis, we may be the least productive we have ever been.

Punchcard perceptions

We’re not working more or fewer hours as a result of IT. It might be more informative to reflect on how we feel about the hours we work.

There’s an interesting train of thought to follow: Why do we work fewer hours (as measured) in software-heavy knowledge work than we used to doing more manual labor? Maybe we reach our limits with mental effort sooner than we would exerting physical effort?

This is evidenced by psychological survey data. The American Psychological Association found that 77% of workers felt stressed at work within the last month, 57% reported negative impacts of work-related stress. Gallup found that globally 41% of employees experienced a lot of stress the previous day (2024 report). 22% of US employees rate their level of burnout as high or very high.

Is “moderate burnout” acceptable? Another 35% of employees fall in that column.

In Gordon’s book, The Rise and Fall of American Growth (2016), he argued that inventions that lead to major productivity gains fundamentally change the nature of the workplace — how businesses operate and how employees execute their work. But with information technology nothing has changed except for increased stress.

Sure, we got cubicles and then the walls of the cubicles came down, we got sent to work from home and then we got called back to the office. Now cubicles are trending again, but through it all we’re still desk jockeys.

Meet the new boss, same as the old boss.

The Productivity Paradox, Revisited

Inspired by Robert Solow’s quip about productivity statistics, the term “Productivity Paradox” was named in 1993 by Erik Brynjolfsson, now a teacher and director at Stanford.

The paradox is said to have disappeared due to the renewed growth we observed in the late 90s, but… I don’t think it ever left. (I also don’t think it’s a paradox at all). It’s still considered controversial to suggest that Information Technology doesn’t deliver the same productivity gains as other General Purpose Technologies like the steam engine and electricity.

Gordon himself acknowledged that productivity growth could have been even worse if somehow software never came to be, but this counterfactual is unknowable. It’s also a bit like giving the little league kids a trophy for showing up — sub-1% TFP growth is no triumph.

One Good Decade, 1995–2004

Before we transport ourselves back in time — à la Bill & Ted — to the 90s, let’s acknowledge the “mismeasurement hypothesis.”

Some commentators suggest that the modern slowdown in productivity is an illusion caused by old data collection methods that ignore the value of free digital goods. Chad Syverson, an economics professor at the University of Chicago, published a thorough rebuttal showing that the slowdown is too large and too synchronized across regions — regardless of their IT consumption — to be explained by digital surplus.

The hard data only supports a brief surge in productivity in the late 90s. Krugman called it an “IT Boom.” It’s commonly accepted that IT gets the credit: Federal Reserve economists Stephen Oliner and Daniel Sichel took the Solow growth-accounting approach and showed that IT capital expenditures and faster computer production were responsible for two-thirds of the growth surge in the 90s. This analysis was published in 2000.

This aligns with other IT-productivity proponents who state that much of our ongoing productivity growth is in the IT industry.

But here’s the problem with that: This is like saying that the greatest benefit of electricity would go to utility companies, or that the breadwinner of internal combustion would be Ford… The whole point of a “general purpose” technology is that it enhances the productivity of many industries, not just its own.

The Federal Reserve analysis is an accounting, not a statement of causality. As the famous Moe Abramovitz quip goes, TFP is a “measure of our ignorance about the causes of economic growth.” And as Oliner & Sichel themselves wrote, the neoclassical “framework provides a superficial explanation of growth.” They went on in their 2000 paper to project that the productivity boost would persist, yet we know it died in 2004 even as IT investment continued to grow.

The Cost Disease

Speaking of accounting, there’s another rival analysis to explain the slowdown in growth over the last half century.

It started with a string quartet.

In 1966, two Williams, Baumol and Bowen, published Performing Arts: The Economic Dilemma. Their original observation was that a Beethoven string quartet requires exactly four musicians and takes exactly as many minutes to perform as it did in 1826. Productivity, in the economic sense, cannot rise without destroying (or changing) that product.

Still, the musicians need their wages to rise along with wages economy-wide or they’ll quit the violin for a job in manufacturing or information technology. The relative cost of the quartet rises forever as other sectors get more efficient and offer higher wages.

This was dubbed the “cost disease,” a strong term, perhaps, but we can guess poor Baumol bemoaned the rising cost of attending the opera. In any profession where human time and attention are the output — a therapy session, a professor’s lecture, a doctor’s exam, a legal consultation — output per hour is capped, wages rise anyway, and the sector’s prices inflate relative to everything else that doesn’t have a capped output.

The “disease” isn’t a dysfunction; it’s just math. These sectors became known as Baumol sectors; we’ll keep coming back to these throughout our exploration.

In 2006, another William, this one with the surname Nordhaus, published Baumol’s Diseases: A Macroeconomic Perspective for the National Bureau of Economic Research. Looking at the previous half century of industry data, he confirmed Baumol’s prediction that “technologically stagnant sectors experience above average cost and price increases, take a rising share of national output, and slow aggregate productivity growth.” Share of GDP shifts to lower growth sectors.

Again this is an accounting, not an explanation of why. It’s also essentially the inverse of the argument that IT does produce productivity growth because the IT industry is growing. Importantly, Baumol sectors got the greatest IT investment (Brookings economists Bosworth & Triplett showed that IT investment goes overwhelmingly to services), which should have resulted in productivity growth, not stagnation, if that was the net effect we expected of IT.

We also have the brief “IT Boom” as evidence that services can register productivity gains with the right blend of circumstances, even if IT itself is not the main ingredient.

Reversion to the Mean

Krugman asked the question too. Why did the “IT Boom” that sorta kinda peaked at previously sustained growth levels only last for a decade? What’s the non-superficial layer, what’s the behavioral variable that explains why the boom lived no longer than a beloved family dog?

A hypothesis: Based on the timing, this boom coincided with the phase of early majority users of the internet (borrowing the framework from Geoffrey Moore’s Crossing the Chasm). And why did it only last a decade? Dare I say it, maybe… Google?

What if, what if, ALL productivity booms are the result of a ménage à trois of access to information, the ability to comprehend that information, and the opportunity for curiosity.

What if the printing press gave us the Renaissance; electrification took us off factory floors and put us in offices; the G.I. Bill gave a generation access to education; and for a brief honeymoon AOL and Yahoo! let us browse the internet.

Then Google got really good at giving us exactly what we were looking for. The insidious thing here is that the easier it is to find the information you’re looking for, the less you discover along the way. This could have massive implications for the long-run results of LLMs.

By contrast, the greatest opportunity cost to human potential is that which detracts from curiosity. We went from read to browse (hypertext! links to more information, like synapses in the brain) to search to chat, and next is delegate.

Browse was the pinnacle (and still can be, for those whose favorite internet experience is Wikipedia), and since then what we are witnessing is a disengagement curve.

I looked for macro evidence to support this hypothesis but it doesn’t cleanly exist. I’ll leave it as is, bounded by italics, to live on as a mere curiosity.

Another coincidence of timing — the World Trade Organization (WTO) opened for business in 1995. Trade openness doesn’t impact the economy immediately, but one thing that does is credit, the fourth element. King and Levine in 1993, “Finance and Growth: Schumpeter Might Be Right,” and Rajan and Zingales in 1998, “Financial Dependence and Growth,” build this case.

The mid-late 90s credit story in the US was Riegle-Neal (1994) opening interstate banking, real rates falling through the decade, retail brokerage and the IPO window opening (bubble acknowledged), and venture funding growing an order of magnitude. This is supporting evidence, not a different theory. Money meets minds.

Efficiencies of information tasks do not lead to productivity, but capital efficiencies do. Oddly enough it may be a sort of information inefficiency that does correlate with productivity growth.

Efficiency vs. Productivity, the Semantic Divide

I’ve tossed out these words repeatedly — efficiency and productivity, without giving them their due attention.

Efficiency is time per task. Micro, measurable, tangible, real. Efficiency is the thing that software empirically delivers. We experience it all day every day, which is why we instinctively overestimate its impact on…

Productivity is value output per hour. Macro, intangible (in our lived experience). What economists measure. The thing that hasn’t budged through fifty years of Information Technology.

It feels logical to connect the two and, in fact, smart people frequently do despite the lack of evidence.

To grab one of a million such statements, here’s pundit Scott Galloway talking about A New AI World, “Starting in the 1980s personal computers put technology that had cost tens of millions 20 years earlier on nearly every person’s desk. The gains in productivity, globally, have been substantial.” (My emphasis).

But, not so. Are you with me on this now?

We now have technology and business luminaries predicting historically unprecedented growth rates thanks to AI. Dario Amodei (Anthropic) envisions a “dream scenario… would be 20% annual GDP growth rate in the developing world,” and touted 10–20% at home. Masayoshi Son expects AI revenue to reach 20% of global GDP by 2040. Marc Andreessen offered the possibility that “productivity growth is about to go through the roof.”

Gross Domestic Product deserves a clarification too: this is all final goods and services produced in a country. Productivity growth is a primary driver of GDP growth. These terms can be misleading to us laypeople. “Product” is value-added output.

Here’s a simple illustrative example: If the world’s pencil powerhouse nation produces 1 billion pencils, but then an AI pencil machine is able to produce 2 billion at the same cost, and sell each of them for half the price, this nation’s GDP will not have changed. Productivity and Product are not measures of cumulative products created, but rather the economic value of those products.

Another example, informally called the “Excel Shock,” gives us a chiaroscuro foreshadowing of what’s to come.

When digital spreadsheets dropped in the late 70s and 80s many expected accounting and finance jobs to be eliminated. What used to require an army of junior automatons could now be done in minutes with Lotus 1–2–3 or Excel. What actually happened instead was an explosion of financial analysis, modeling, forecasting, and reporting. Finance jobs expanded and up-leveled, but meanwhile the lack of macro productivity gains during this period was one of the more visible paradoxical surprises to economists.

Producing more does not mean growth. AI will produce more — we see that already, but will producing more lead to greater Product and Productivity growth? The instinctive hunch we feel is that the answer should be yes, but this treatise seeks to prove that the answer will be no.

It’s not just productivity growth that has been the subject of sensational predictions, there’s also the drastic reduction in work — the promised utopia.

Where did the [predictions of] good times go?

In 1930, John Maynard Keynes famously speculated that within a century technology would enable us to work 15 hour weeks. 2030 is right around the corner…

In 1956 Nixon anticipated a four-day work week. Larry Page, belatedly, predicted the reduced work week in 2014 (maybe he Googled it?).

What do we think of Jamie Dimon predicting a three-and-a-half-day work week? Lame one-upsmanship. He put it rather eloquently, “literally they’ll probably be working three and a half days a week.” He also said AI is a “living breathing thing,” so… yeah, can I apply to be the CEO of Chase?

The fallacies driving these poor predictions are the same ones that support our conviction that software makes us more productive. But it doesn’t.

And yet this is unsettling. These are brilliant and/or highly competent thinkers and leaders and they’re wildly wrong, going on a century now. I find it unsettling.

Cognitive dissonance

We experience the efficiency of using software and we can recognize that each new generation of computers and software is a leap forward in power and efficiency. Surely this should let us increase productivity?

Gordon Moore’s prediction — the number of transistors on a microchip would double every two years — was remarkably accurate. Two to the Nth power is quite powerful.

Here are some data points on the number of transistors on a microchip:

  • 1965: ~64 transistors
  • 1971 (Intel 4004): 2,300 transistors
  • 1982 (Intel 80286): 134,000 transistors
  • 1993 (Intel Pentium): 3.1 million transistors
  • 2006 (Intel Core 2 Duo): 291 million transistors
  • 2018 (AMD Ryzen 7 2700X): 4.8 billion transistors
  • 2023 (Apple M2 Ultra): 134 billion transistors

Total increase since 1965: Over 2 billion (~2.1x10⁹) times more transistors per chip.

We’ve made use of those chips to increase computing power even faster.

  • 1971 (Intel 4004): ~1 kFLOPS (floating point emulated in software)
  • 1982 (Intel 80286 + 80287 coprocessor): ~50 kFLOPS
  • 1993 (Intel Pentium): ~75 MFLOPS
  • 2006 (Intel Core 2 Duo): ~15 GFLOPS
  • 2018 (NVIDIA V100, as the frontier moved from CPU to GPU): ~125 TFLOPS
  • 2023 (NVIDIA H100): ~2,000 TFLOPS (2 petaFLOPS at the low precision AI runs on)

Total increase since 1971: Over 1 trillion times (10¹²) increase in computing power.

Let’s visualize this on a logarithmic scale:

If we looked at this without the log scale we’d be looking at a 90 degree angle with a corner radius. Let’s appreciate for a moment that the y-axis goes to 10-to-the-15th. We should be wizards by now.

What gives?

The Audit

We’ve got a trillion-fold increase in input, accelerating every day. We’ve got measurable, observed, felt efficiency gains. We’ve got flat hours (and worse mornings). And yet we have decelerating output growth. The books still balance to near zero.

Where did that trillion-fold increase in computational power go, in the macroeconomics? Something absorbed the dividend.

We’ve looked at the defenses and the apologists and the just-wait-any-day-now crowd. I’m not buying their argument that the gains just haven’t landed on the books yet.

Software does not — and here I’ll add the uncomfortable part — will not lead to productivity growth. If you stay with us through the end of this treatise, we’ll argue why this will hold with AI and even AGI.

For forty years we’ve called it a paradox, as if the books simply failed to balance. But the paradox isn’t a paradox, we’ve just been looking in the wrong direction. The books always balance. If a trillion fold increase in computation didn’t buy us productivity, it bought something else — something that compounds, something that shows up as more windows, more tabs, more systems, more steps between us and done. There’s a word for it, and it isn’t ‘growth.’

Friends, Medium’s algorithm won’t necessarily surface subsequent parts of this treatise for you. I’ll do my best to make each part a standalone article, but if you do want to read the whole thing there are a couple actions that might help: Save Part 1 and check back (I’ll add links to each part after publication) or Follow with email notifications on.

title: The feature was fine. So why did users keep hiding it?
text:
The feature was fine. So why did users keep hiding it?

The retention killer that never shows up in a requirements doc.

The room was in Seoul, quiet except for the hum of the air conditioner. Behind the one-way mirror, product planners sat with notebooks, in the years before K-beauty shook the world. Then one sentence broke the silence.

“If my boyfriend gives me this brand as a gift, that’s his way of telling me he wants to break up.”

Every participant in the room nodded, as if on cue. The second sentence hit even harder.

“The lipstick has incredible color payoff. But I take just the product out and transfer it into a Chanel case before I carry it.”

Lipstick is the one cosmetic that lives in public view. Its case isn’t packaging. It’s an accessory, in the same category as a watch or a wallet. A Chanel case was the smallest unit of luxury she could actually own, and the cheapest tool available for defending her identity in front of other people. She hadn’t rejected the product: she loved the color payoff and used it every day. What she rejected was the signal the brand sent to everyone watching. With her own hands, she’d taken a knife to it and cut function clean away from identity.

Fabricio Teixeira has made a related point about out-of-box experience: what happens after purchase is still part of the product experience, and physical touchpoints continue carrying the brand story. MISSHA showed what happens when that story clashes with the user’s own identity.

Translate that into product terms: core feature satisfaction, off the charts. Repurchase and referral intent, on the floor. Run the usability tests, mine the open-ended NPS responses, and the reason never surfaces. It’s the wall every planner eventually hits, staring at a requirements doc that has nothing wrong with it.

Same spec sheet, completely different retention.

MISSHA opened the “roadshop” category at a startling $3 a product, and grew from a single Korean brand into one now sold across more than 40 countries. LANEIGE sat in the same affordable range, but it occupied a completely different place in consumers’ minds. An Amorepacific brand now sold through Sephora in more than twenty countries, it was never expensive, but never embarrassing to pull out in public either.

The price gap between the two brands was negligible, and their ingredient lists were close enough that no spec comparison would explain the difference. Then latecomers arrived at the same price point and layered on identity. One built a store experience like a princess’s dressing room; another filled every touchpoint with a consistent nature-first message. That’s where the crack started.

The question in every product review meeting was always the same: “What feature do we add to lift retention?” The question itself was wrong. The spec deck, packed card after card, was missing nothing. The requirements doc, by design, was never built to hold the axis of “how do I look to other people, using this?”

Why identity feedback never makes it into a spec.

The raw voices from the repositioning research didn’t pull punches.

Hearing “tacky” and “embarrassing” puts a planner in a bind. A usability problem, like “I can’t find the button,” has a clear owner and a clear fix. An identity problem has no owner. It’s scattered across the logo, the copy, the tone of voice, and the store lighting. It’s impossible to cut into a single Scrum ticket.

Then came the sentence that flipped the table.

“Among affordable brands, Laneige is one I can take out in front of my boyfriend without embarrassment, but MISSHA is not.”

No standard benchmarking data, no quantitative metric, will ever catch that gap. Delivering “this looks tacky” straight to the executives who built the brand made for a silent debrief room. But the project succeeded for one reason: feedback nobody could quantify still got put at the top of the roadmap, instead of filed away in an appendix. The harder step was organizational: leadership chose not to defend the brand against the research. They treated the discomfort as evidence to work with, rather than something to explain away.

Launched in 2000, MISSHA was one of Korea’s original affordable beauty pioneers, helping establish the one-brand-shop model that became a defining part of early K-beauty.

The axis missing from the priority matrix.

One useful way to translate Jennifer Aaker’s brand-personality theory into UX terms is to think about two axes at once.

The function axis: does this solve my problem?
The identity axis: what does using this say about me to other people?

The identity mismatch can run in two directions: who users believe they are and who they want to become. MISSHA fit neither. In those sessions, it represented a version of the self they were trying to leave behind.

The requirements docs, feature specs, and competitive matrices we write cover almost only the first axis. The second gets waved off with “brand or design will handle it.”

But the real switch that flips churn is the second axis. Function can be excellent, and if the identity score is low, users hide the product: no screenshots, no mentions on social, quietly buried two pages deep in a home-screen folder. When the identity axis is strong, users will happily tolerate real functional flaws.

This pattern is playing out right now. A KPMG and University of Melbourne study of 48,000 respondents across 47 countries found that 57% of employees admit to hiding their AI use at work. In a controlled Atlassian experiment, identical work was rated far lazier the moment it was disclosed as AI-assisted. High satisfaction and concealed usage: the same structure as a lipstick moved into a Chanel case.

How a single raw sentence rewrote the roadmap.

MISSHA’s recovery started right there. The repositioning concept, “Bold Beauty,” came straight out of those sessions, and every touchpoint was rebuilt around a single ideal-user image: a confident career woman living on her own terms. Trace any decision back far enough and it lands on a sentence a consumer actually said out loud. Not a metric. A sentence was the basis for the roadmap.

3 actionable steps for your next sprint

  1. Add an identity axis to the priority matrix. Next to the impact-effort matrix, ask one more question: does this feature reinforce the user’s ideal self-image? Nielsen Norman Group’s State of UX 2026 makes a related point: as design systems and standardization make competent UI easier to produce, surface-level interface quality is becoming less of a differentiator. That makes the identity axis harder to dismiss as “just branding.”
  2. Add “did you hide it?” to your churn interviews. “Why did you stop using this?” only returns predictable feature complaints. Add: “Have you ever told a coworker or friend you use this app?” and “Have you ever screenshotted this screen to share it with someone?” If usability is fine but people are reluctant to show it off, that service is quietly sitting on a time bomb.
  3. Put unquantified sentences on the roadmap agenda. We’re in an era where AI summarizes thousands of VOC entries in seconds. But Nielsen Norman Group’s research on AI-generated review summaries found that even well-designed summaries fail to answer the specific question a user actually cared about — customers kept clicking back to individual reviews to find the exact detail the summary had smoothed over. A sentence like “I’m embarrassed to use this in front of my boyfriend” gets reduced, in the summary, to a flat line like “brand image needs improvement.” What flips the table isn’t a summarized chart. It’s a user’s raw sentence.

Closing

Identity isn’t an extra line item to hand off to the brand team. It has to come into the product document as its own axis. Leave it out, and even the most polished feature eventually becomes replaceable.

Picture the product you’re building right now. Does the user proudly pull it up in public, or quietly bury it two pages deep in a folder?

This article draws on consumer research the author advised on during a Korean beauty brand’s revitalization project, and reflects participant perceptions within a specific research context and point in time.

title: Virgo Season Is Here — & You’re Entering A Fresh Era
text:
Virgo Season Is Here — & You’re Entering A Fresh Era

It’s Virgo season! From August 22nd to September 22nd, the sun will be in the empathetic, wise, patient, and nurturing sign of Virgo. This period of the year always makes us nostalgic for the shavings of No. 2 pencils from elementary school perfuming the air (since class is in session), the turning of the leaves as summer ends and fall begins, and the juncture to start rewatching Gilmore Girls for the hundredth time before cozy season begins. If we’re lucky, we can have one more epic beach day with friends.

Now, we are leaning into our inventiveness and altruistic era. We are analyzing situations to get to the bottom of them and being communicative to bring clarity to matters. At times, we might be somewhat critical and stubborn, but that’s just because we want everything to be perfect when the sun is in Virgo. The key to surviving and thriving is to comprehend that we have to lighten up and not be so serious. 

Virgo season hits a little differently this year. In the past, we’ve been dealing with harsh aspects from Saturn and Neptune’s stint in Pisces; however, this time around, we are not harnessing the tense push and pull between these two planets on the sun. Not to say that we aren’t going to experience minor frustrations because, well, that’s just life. The vibes are more positive and pleasant now, allowing us to have an amazing last month of summer.

The first week of Virgo season is the only dramatic part that we’re going to be dealing with. August 28th marks the day of the lunar eclipse in Pisces, which requires us to embrace radical self-love. The sun in Virgo and moon in Pisces will square rebellious Uranus in Gemini, making the events of this day shocking and unpredictable. The mutable energy makes us all uncertain of the next steps forward, but it also gives us the energy to go with the flow and transcend into newness. 

The lunar eclipse is part of the last chapter of the story we’ve been dealing with for the past year and a half. With the North Node of Destiny beginning its journey on July 26th, we are in a fresh era, one that is full of possibility and the chance to manifest our fate. As a result, we are feeling ourselves, boosting our confidence and bravado. Anything is possible under the lunar eclipse. One portal closes and another opens. The good news is that Mercury cazimi in Virgo (the sun and Mercury’s inspiring conjunction) occurs on August 27th, the day before the eclipse, lighting up our minds and hearts with pureness and clarity. 

The rest of the month focuses on healing. We are looking for alternative ways to support and lift spirits to evolve. It’s been a long summer full of heartache and frustration, so think of this time as a pristine moment to try different modalities that motivate growth on a soulful level. For all we know, it can become our new go-to. The lesson is to try novel and original methods. The greatest flex is to be daring and adventurous — even if that only means choosing a different matcha latte flavor. The results could be magnificent or icky. But, unless we try, we’ll never know.

Obviously, we should proceed with caution; dipping our toes in the water before jumping in is the best way to exhibit and embrace the energy of Virgo season. Collect the data before responding and making assumptions.

August 22nd: The sun enters Virgo, starring a four-week trip for the earth sign around the sun.

August 25th: Mercury moves into Virgo, marking a pristine moment to catch up on errands, emails, and connections. 

August 28th: The lunar eclipse in Pisces urges us to break free from the past and move into the future.

September 10th: Venus swims into Scorpio, heightening our passions and expectations of others. 

September 10th: Mercury glides into Libra, making communication easy and direct. 

September 10th: Uranus retrograde in Gemini allows us to reflect on the way we use our words to express our thoughts and desires.

September 10th: The New Moon in Virgo offers a flash of discernment and sagacity that enhances our auras.

title: “She Saved My Life”: 5 Women On Learning To Reach Out To Their Friends
text:
“She Saved My Life”: 5 Women On Learning To Reach Out To Their Friends Warning: This article discusses grief, illness and death.

How many times have you looked at your friend’s number on your phone, your thumb hovering over the dial button...then felt you couldn’t disturb them and locked the screen? Years ago, when my mom had to spend a couple of weeks in the hospital, I found myself doing just that. I’ve done it more times than I can remember. It’s easy to feel like the weight and responsibility of being there for someone when it’s really dark is reserved for partners, not friends. Society, after all, places more emotional emphasis on romance than friendship. It doesn’t always feel appropriate to call a friend and ask them to come over because you can’t bear to go home to an empty house, or face a diagnosis, or because you simply need to cry with someone. I remember all those years ago, standing in the dark under a billboard with my phone in hand, feeling as though it wasn’t fair to reach out to a friend, because friends don’t sign up to this kind of thing. Looking back, I was so wrong.

The Room Next Door recently hit big screens and what struck me when I went to see it was the gravity of what we can ask of our friends, how we do it, and how intimate platonic relationships can become in times of need. In the film, Tilda Swinton’s character, Martha, who is dying of cancer, makes the biggest possible request of another person, and it’s her friend Ingrid (Julianne Moore) who receives this request — there is no romantic partner to lean on. The film looks at how their friendship grows and is challenged in equal measure by Martha's request and Ingrid's desire to help. I left the screening feeling as though we should all be a bit braver within our friendships and ask for help when we need it — even if we feel the ask is big. 

Refinery29 spoke to women about the times their friends rose to the occasion and didn’t make them feel burdensome. Often it’s our friends who understand us best and know what we need when the time comes. I’ve grown to learn this in the last couple of years, and if I could go back to that night when my mom was first staying in hospital, I’d have reached out to my friend. Now, when problems arrive that I can’t solve alone, I press the dial button. Support is always there.

title: Fenty Beauty’s New Pro Filt’r Foundation Is Here—and Yes, It’s Even Better Than the OG
text:
Fenty Beauty’s New Pro Filt’r Foundation Is Here—and Yes, It’s Even Better Than the OG

I’ll never forget the first time I bought makeup at Sephora. It was a few weeks before my 21st birthday, and one of my best friends came along to help me shop for my first-ever full glam (before then, lip gloss was about as far as I’d ventured). I knew immediately that I wanted to use Fenty Beauty, and my makeup-obsessed bestie happily helped me find my perfect match in the brand’s matte foundation. Six years later, my love affair with Rihanna’s iconic namesake label is still going strong—its Instant Retouch Concealer and now-discontinued bronzer included. Naturally, its newest innovation, the Fenty Beauty Pro Filt’r Fluid Flex Natural Matte Longwear Foundation, has already earned a permanent spot on my makeup shelf. 

After launching in 2017 with a then-rare 40-shade range, Fenty Beauty helped raise the bar for what inclusive complexion products could look like. Nearly a decade later, its new foundation proves the brand isn’t done pushing the category forward.

Ahead, I get into a full digest of everything there is to know about Pro Filt’r Fluid Flex Foundation, and why I’m obsessed with it (and you will be, too).

What Makes Fenty’s New Foundation Different?

If you’ve used the brand’s Pro Filt’r Soft Matte Longwear Foundation, you can think of Fluid Flex as a similar product, but all grown up. It’s not only breathable and delivers an impressive matte finish, but it’s powered by polymer technology that merges skincare and makeup seamlessly. This innovative, non-comedogenic formulation works to resist water and sebum, minimize fine lines and pores, protect the skin barrier, and create that natural, blurring effect—even for the most oily-skinned girl (me). Not to mention, Fluid Flex comes in an all-new 50-shade range that caters to undertones for an even more accurate match. 

I Put Fenty’s New Foundation To The Test

As I mentioned before, Fenty Beauty’s original foundation was the first one I ever used, and it’s still a mainstay in my regimen. The new formula is even more of a favorite, because it truly does what it claims to do. As a (sometimes) proud normal-to-oily skin girly, I’ve had my fair share of complexion products that actually help me conquer excess sebum, and ones that simply don’t, despite their claims. I made sure to wear Fluid Flex in environments where I knew its staying power would truly be tested—a girls’ night out on the town with my friend on a very humid Friday, and the final night of Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” residency at Madison Square Garden, where I was dancing and singing my heart out. And let’s just say, my face was still intact without any transfer anywhere by the end of both occasions.

Being able to find an exact match in the shade 456W for my complexion was satisfying, to say the least. It’s more than clear that the brand went back to the drawing board for this range, intentionally putting all undertones and skin tones first. My skin is proof of that—and it doesn’t just look like skin; it feels like it, too.

– Available in 50 shades to match undertones
– Formulated in a hydrating, waterproof and matte finish
– Offers medium, buildable coverage for up to 12-hour wear
– Ingredients include starfruit extract for all-day oil control

As with anything Fenty Beauty creates, Pro Filt’r Fluid Flex Foundation is relatively easy to use. A little really does go a long way, so I use one pump and blend it into my skin. I used my OG foundation brush, but you can even get better results with the Fluid Flex Foundation Brush 165.

If you’re looking for more coverage, feel free to apply another pump and blend as desired. You can also use a setting spray like the You Mist Makeup-Extending Setting Spray before completing the rest of your makeup for that extra matte effect. Either way, you’re bound to get the blurred, skin-like look that, as you can see, does everything but disappoint.

If your skin tends to get oily or you’re prone to breakouts, Pro Filt’r Fluid Flex is a foundation worth trying. It looks and feels like skin, enhancing my natural features without making me feel like I’ve altered my appearance—which is exactly my kind of glam. It makes me feel my most beautiful and confident, and that’s no shocker. Rihanna’s behind it, after all.

Starting September 4, Pro Filt’r Fluid Flex Foundation will retail for $48 and be available on Fenty Beauty’s website, Sephora, Ulta, and Kohl’s.

title: A Week In Wichita, KS On $22.06 An Hour
text:
A Week In Wichita, KS On $22.06 An Hour

Welcome to Money Diaries where we are tackling the ever-present taboo that is money. We’re asking real people how they spend their hard-earned money during a seven-day period — and we’re tracking every last dollar.

This week: A teller working in banking who makes $22.06 an hour and spends some of it on a custom poem.

If you’d like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we’re not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.

This diary was written in 2026.

Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We’d love to hear your thoughts here.

Occupation: Teller
Industry: Banking
Age: 23
Location: Wichita, KS
Salary: $22.06/hr
Joint Income/Financial Setup: My spouse makes between $22-25/hr, so combined, we bring home around $70k per year after tax. We have a joint checking account for groceries/eating out and pet expenses, as well as a joint savings account for travel. We contribute the same amount to our checking account every month ($600 each). All other money is separate. We love having the joint checking since it makes any small purchases or eating out really easy — without having to keep track of who owes what.
Assets:
Checking: ~$450 (I contribute $300 biweekly and my spouse contributes $150 weekly)
High-Yield Savings: $9,721.72
401(k): $8,623.70 (this is a combined value with my Roth)
Car (KBB value): ~$18,000
Debt: $0
Paycheck Amount (biweekly): ~$1170 ($1,700 minus taxes, pet insurance, 10% 401(k) contribution, and 5% Roth contribution)
Pronouns: They/them

Monthly Expenses

Housing Costs: $575 (one-bed, one-bathroom townhouse — plus pet rent, split evenly with my spouse)
Loan Payments: $0 (I have one CC that I put larger purchases on to get cash back, but I pay them the same day they post)
Utilities: $50-100 (gas and electric, depending on time of year, split evenly)
Internet: $0 (we both have unlimited data on our phones and use our mobile hotspots to save money)
Phone: $30 ($360 prepaid yearly for unlimited data with Mint Mobile)
Car: $160 (insurance, tags, oil changes, and gas)
Compost: $6 (split with spouse)
Google One: $2.99

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
It was definitely assumed that I would go to college. My dad is highly educated, and my mom got her bachelor’s degree. Although I’m sure they wouldn’t have been opposed to me going to a trade school or something, college was just the default. For their generation, it was worth the cost and time, but now it’s not guaranteed you’ll make more, or even be able to pay back your loans. They told me my whole life that they would cover tuition or room and board, so if I could study hard and get a full tuition scholarship, I could go to school for free. I ended up getting a half-ride at a small liberal arts college, and paid for the room and board with a combination of savings, campus/summer research/off-campus jobs. Since I got a half-ride, my parents did contribute some money to my housing, and I did graduate with my bachelor’s degree debt-free, which is an immense blessing.

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
My mom is really into finance and always managed the money in our house. She tried to teach me about the value of money from a young age. I was raised religious, so any money I made doing chores around the house had 10% go toward tithing, 50% to savings, and 40% to what she called “fun money.” If I wanted to go to the mall with my friends or get something from the store, it came from that. I also remember her telling me to open a credit card at a young age to build credit, but to never spend money I didn’t have (that advice apparently didn’t stick; I got into upwards of $2K at one point and $5K at another in credit card debt in my life, all of which I have since paid off).

What was your first job and why did you get it?
I babysat for families in the church growing up for pocket money, but my first taxable job was during the summer at 16, working as a host at a chain restaurant for $4/hr plus tipshare. Quite literally, it is the hardest job I ever had in my life. I got it because I wanted to save for college and my parents wanted me to get work experience.

Did you worry about money growing up?
I don’t know that I was worried, but I was definitely aware. My dad was in school during my childhood, and my mom didn’t work, so I knew that there were things we “couldn’t afford.” I think things were tighter than I knew, but they made things work. We would go out somewhere to eat like Taco Bell on birthdays, but otherwise never ate out. Every other year we drove twenty-plus hours to visit family, but otherwise we didn’t go on vacations. We got hand-me-down clothes from friends or family, or went to thrift stores. It just seemed normal then, but now that my dad makes more, they can afford a lot more. My siblings are all younger and I’m the only one who remembers it being different. My mom is still very frugal and particular with how they use their money, and they save a lot but they go on a lot of nice trips and eat out weekly, which is just kind of shocking to me.

Do you worry about money now?
I’m thankful to have the means to provide for my lifestyle and have some leftover, but I’m very conscious that I have no choice but to work. I have an emergency fund built up that would last me about six months of unemployment, and I know I’m lucky enough to have a safety net in my family and spouse, but capitalism is just scary. I’m currently thinking about moving to part-time work to pursue writing as a career more seriously, which we can afford, but it does worry me. I’m aware I don’t really have that much in savings or my 401(k). It’s really important to me that I’m able to retire, and I care more about being able to work fewer hours and still make the same income than increasing my income.

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
I was pretty much responsible for myself in college. Other than the half of tuition my parents provided, I covered my rent/board and living expenses. I always paid my own insurance and tags for the car my parents let me drive, as well as my phone bill. I would say true financial independence happened at 22 when I’d had my own place for over a year, and got my own insurance and phone plan, instead of paying my mom back. If I really needed it, I think they would be a safety net for me, but I would like to avoid that at all costs.

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
As mentioned above, my parents paid for my college tuition, which I’m very grateful for. They also bought a car during my last year of college after I broke up with my long-time partner and didn’t have a way of getting to school out-of-state. They ended up giving me this car, paid off, which was unexpected, and I’m so lucky to have. My parents also offered $10K towards my wedding, which we ended up using ~$8K of.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day One: Tuesday

7:09 a.m. — Get out of bed. Morning routine using my spouse C.’s phone to do my Duolingo lesson (461 days of Spanish) and read my horoscope on CoStar, then brush my teeth and snuggle with C. and cat, Y. You can safely assume I’ll do this every day. I put out some food for Y. She’s on a prescription diet after a health scare, so it’s dry in the morning and canned in the evening. I already packed my breakfast yesterday and this week my work is providing lunch, so I kiss C. and head out.

8:30 a.m. — I snack on the breakfast I bring to work every day (fruit, cheese, peanut butter). It’s kind of a busy morning with calls but I do the LinkedIn and NYT games and manage to read a bit of the book I brought. I’ve read 52 books this year already.

12 p.m. — Eat the free lunch, which is surprisingly good. We very rarely get lunch paid for at my work, but this week has a lot of organizational/system changes happening, so they’re treating us. I sit in my car while I eat and read.

5:03 p.m. — It’s been a slower day, thankfully, after some busy weeks. I finish my book and rate it three stars. I try to start the other book I brought but after one sentence it’s clear I’m not going to like it. Yesterday, I was stuck here until almost 6 p.m. because of a system error, so I’m out a little bit earlier than usual today. I stop by the library on the way home to return the two books I brought to work today and pick up a hold.

6:00 p.m. — C. and I start on dinner — shrimp scampi. We are both gluten-free and don’t exactly love cooking, so dinner can sometimes be a struggle. Thankfully, we’ve been on a pretty good streak. It doesn’t sit well with me tonight, though. C. puts out the wet food for Y. We chat about what C. is going to do this evening. Today is a writing day for me. I have a novel I’ve been working on for the better part of a decade that is finally nearing a state where I can start querying agents. It’s definitely been a learning curve figuring out what pursuing writing while working full-time and spending time with C. and family looks like. We’ve settled on selecting a few days a week for me to focus on writing in the evening while C. hangs out with their family or works on their own projects. They decide to go to a baseball game with their family.

9:30 p.m. — C. gets back. I’m done writing for the night after getting a good amount of work done. I set a goal date to start querying and put down this draft, which is coming up in about ten days, and I feel good about making that deadline. We talk and catch up since we didn’t get to see each other much earlier. I take a quick shower with a shower cap on before falling asleep sometime around 10:45.

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Two: Wednesday

7:11 a.m. — Typical morning routine using C.’s phone since I have a flip phone. I bought a flip phone at the beginning of 2025 when C. and I decided to quit social media as a New Year’s resolution. We ended up deleting our accounts but didn’t end up switching to flip phones since it seemed like a big jump. In July 2025, my phone broke and I decided to just try it out rather than buying a new phone. Now, it’s been nearly a year and other than using C.’s phone for Duolingo and banking apps, I rely solely on it.

11:05 a.m. — Lunch. We all come back to eat and chat while it’s slow for a second. C. texts me about a potential lead for a part-time job starting in the fall. I’m considering working part-time for a year so I can focus on writing and applying to an MFA program that would start next fall. For a year, we can definitely make the part-time work, and this job would be close to my house and I can potentially bike to it, so we could cut costs with only one car.

1:49 p.m. — Today has been slower, too. Over lunch, I start my new book, the hold I picked up yesterday. I text with the potential job and it sounds like it could definitely be a good fit, values-wise. It feels like a sign that I only decided to start looking two days ago, and this is checking every box, but I try not to get my hopes up.

5:30 p.m. — I call C. on my way home and they’re still at our friend D.’s house picking up a book for book club and chatting. They have made plans to hang while I write tonight, since it’s another writing day for me. I head home to start dinner — elote pasta salad, with some reheated leftovers from work. C. gets home pretty soon after me and we chat about our days. They are really excited about the potential job, and we set up a time to meet with the lead next week. C. works in the same field so they are invited to come along.

6:40 p.m. — Our downstairs neighbor texts C. that the yoga mat on our balcony fell into our yard again and that our other neighbor has a poster for us. We go down to chat with her. She’s the nicest older lady ever. The poster turns out to be from a few years ago for an event in our community. It’s sweet he thought of us and I put the poster up immediately. D. picks up C. to go pick up art supplies and snacks for a party C. is throwing this weekend.

8:45 p.m. — I finish up the chapter I’m writing and realize I only have one, potentially two, depending on how I go about it, more to write. This slightly terrifies me, so I call it a night and start watching movie trailers on YouTube. There’s a couple of funny ones that I decide we need to watch. C. gets home, gives me a haul of all the snacks she got and we catch up before getting in bed around 9:45 and zonking out pretty quickly.

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Three: Thursday

7:05 a.m. — Get out of bed, morning snuggles and phone time. I get sucked into looking at old pictures. I’m leaving a bit later today (still correcting the overtime from Monday), so C. and I sit out on the balcony chatting about the part-time job until I have to leave. I get to work, eat my breakfast, and start doing calls. Thankfully, we’re almost caught up on the backlog of these and I won’t have to do as many soon. My boss’s boss comes down with candy, which I accept.

11:57 a.m. — We’ve had system issues all morning and it’s been moderately stressful. I’m glad it’s lunchtime. I read in my car and eat. When I come back from lunch, the issues have gotten worse, and it’s pretty busy for a while. I finish the book from yesterday and rate it four stars, barely. It started strong but didn’t really stick the landing.

3:55 p.m. — I journal intermittently about the ending for my novel since I’m still feeling anxious about writing it. It’s daunting to be so close to a sort of end, even if there’s plenty more to do in terms of edits if/when I get an agent. The querying stage will be much more nebulous. I write about my fears of not doing the story justice and what isn’t seeming to click right now in the narrative, which gives me an idea for what to do instead. It all kind of flows from there, and I outline for this weekend when I’ll have some writing time.

5:30 p.m. — Get home from work and C. has made stuffed peppers (without the peppers, so basically ground beef, rice, cream cheese, and tomato sauce). We eat, I load the dishwasher, and then we head to our rock climbing class. We just started this month and we’ve loved it. It was $60 a piece for four lessons, prepaid. We’re the only adults in the class and this week some of the kids didn’t show up either, so we get a lot more opportunities to climb. A kid asks what the best time is for one of the courses and the instructor says the fastest he’s timed is 35 seconds. For shits and giggles, I try it and get 38 seconds and briefly feel like I’m about to be scouted for my abilities.

7:55 p.m. — After class I grab a sparkling soda from a local drink place ($3.17, but I have $15.18 in cash back on my credit card) and we walk around the nearby nature preserve. The weather is really nice and we end up talking and sitting watching the water pretty late.

9:15 p.m. — Get home and C. realizes they’re not at all ready for the party this weekend. I take a shower and then help them set up before we get sucked into looking at my aunt’s Facebook and finding really old pictures of me from ten years ago. Lay down around 10:40 p.m. and fall asleep around 11:15 p.m.

Daily Total: $0

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Four: Friday

7:13 a.m. — Get out of bed. Definitely stayed up a bit too late last night. C. feeds Y. as I do my usual morning stuff. C. is tired and not in the best mood so I put on a song and do a corny dance. We keep listening to music while they eat breakfast and I pack my bag. We’re both in a good mood by the time I leave. When I get to work, I withdraw $20 from the ATM before I clock in. C. and I are going to a poetry open mic tonight with a suggested admission of $10 a piece. This comes from our joint checking, so my total is $10. It’s a busy morning and a client has made a complaint about something that wasn’t in my control. I try not to let it get under my skin. $10

9:57 a.m. — The deadline I gave myself to start querying is in one week. I bite the bullet and get a month’s subscription to a website about publishing deals for my querying research ($30 on my credit card, which still has $12.01 in cash back). It bothers me how much information in publishing is behind paywalls but I consider it an investment. I schedule it to cancel my membership before it charges me for another month and will decide then if it’s worth the money. $17.99

11:38 a.m. — I get a text that our electric bill is ready, so I go in and pay it. It’s $125.14 (already included in utilities above). Sigh. Gone are the months of winter/spring where we could squeak by paying $50-$75/month. I eat lunch in my car and start my new book. The hours after my lunch are so busy, and it’s not over yet. Usually there’s another rush around 3:30/4. I’m very grateful it’s Friday.

4:59 p.m. — It gets worse. Finally, I clock out and head home to feed Y. C. and I eat some leftovers before driving over to the poetry event. We park and I pay for two hours of parking through the app ($2.35 on joint card) and immediately realize the default license plate is C.’s old car. I moan and groan a little bit about having to do two more hours with the correct license plate ($2.35 on joint card) before we go inside. We give them our $20 donation and roam around the gallery before sitting down. There are art supplies at the tables and we chat with some strangers while collaging. $2.35

8:05 p.m. — I realize we’re probably going to need to extend the parking for another hour ($1.35 on joint card) so I do that before going up and reading two poems. I’m slightly nervous but they’re received well! We sit through the rest and have a lot of fun before heading home. I work on laundry while C. sets up for the party. I’m pretty tired and not in the greatest mood as I help and we end up going to bed soon after. I fall asleep pretty fast. $0.67

Daily Total: $31.01

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Five: Saturday

7:45 a.m. — C. comes in to snuggle and ask if I want them to start breakfast. I say yes and get in the shower while they make French toast, hashbrown patties, and eggs. We eat and move Y.’s stuff into the room. We set up all the food and supplies for the party.

10:05 a.m. — People are going to be late and C. gets a bit sad, but then everyone shows up in a big clump and I head into the office to write. I get about a thousand words written. C. grabs me to set up the projector to show everyone pictures. The first thing one of our friends says is, “Where’s the book?!” which is funny. I hang out with everyone until they have to leave so we can eat lunch and get ready to go to a musical (previously paid for, ~$84)

1:45 p.m. — Get to the musical and realize they moved us but the seats we originally had were by some family friends! We get a really yummy mocktail ($4.30 plus $1 tip on joint card) and end up moving to sit with them after intermission. They mention that their oldest has a pretty big role in a musical coming up next month. $2.65

5:15 p.m. — We get home and buy tickets to see the musical they mentioned ($90 from joint savings). $45

7:45 p.m. — It’s really hot and we decide to go swimming. We grab food on the way ($32.72 on joint card). C. and I swim for a while with my siblings before the weather starts to look kind of dicey. We end up playing some games inside with my family while it starts raining, hoping for the weather to blow over, but it just gets worse. $16.36

9:20 p.m. — Finally head home. Thankfully, it’s not actively raining but there’s so much lightning and the streets are kind of flooded. We are both tired but wound for sound and have a hard time getting to bed.

Daily Total: $64.01

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Six: Sunday

8:15 a.m. — I’m exhausted this morning. C. gets in the shower and I feed Y. and do my usual morning stuff. I started doing French lessons yesterday out of novelty and do three more today since they’re basic. We decide we’re going to bike to a coffee shop to get breakfast before going to a Pride event today. We get all dressed up and head out. On the way there, we run into N., a friend we haven’t seen in a while who is walking over to the event. We tell them we’ll see them there.

9:40 a.m. — Food finally comes out and we are #hangry. C. paid for the food on their card because we realized it’s the only card we brought but when we get home I’ll transfer everything I owe (my half is $13.79). After fueling up and refilling the water bottle, we bike over to the event. Pretty much immediately we run into N. who is there with a friend, too. We wander around with them and run into D. and a few other people we know. C. gets some stickers and tea and we share a mango limeade (my half is $2.50). We then run into C.’s boss and they chat for a while. N. and their friend are hungry but C. and I are still wanting to walk around so we part ways. $16.29

11:40 a.m. — I run into someone I know from a local writing group. I’ve missed several meetups because I’ve been busy, but we catch up a little and I end up getting a custom poem from them ($21.20). We also catch up with a musician friend performing. C. finds a really pretty frame which we get since we’re trying to make a gallery wall in our living room (my half is $5), and then we grab some herbs from the apothecary (my half is $5.29). I run into another person from writing group and start to feel like maybe I do live in a small town. We start to get hot and hungry so we bike home. $31.49

12:45 p.m. — I take a shower first thing. Then we have some lunch and C. figures out what I owe them and I send it to them. While we’re sitting there, I order our groceries for the coming week — everything we need for breakfast/lunch as well as four dinners. We’re trying out a different store and they have a deal for $30 off your first order, and with some other coupons, $130 worth of food ends up being $64.28 (on joint card). We will pick this up tomorrow after work. $32.14

4:40 p.m. — Get some much-needed chill time at home before C. and I head over to have dinner at my family’s house. We play board games and hang out before leaving a bit earlier than usual since we were there late yesterday.

8:20 p.m. — Get home and prep for the coming week. Go to sleep at a decent time and fall asleep around 10 p.m., thank God.

Daily Total: $79.92

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Seven: Monday

7:00 a.m. — Snuggle with C. when the alarm goes off until we have to get up. Usual morning routine. I’m still doing French even though I find the way words are pronounced really funny. Pack my lunch and I’m off to work. It’s a pretty typical morning. I crush the Wordle in two guesses, get no mistakes in Connections, and use no hints in Strands. This makes me feel unnecessarily accomplished.

10:05 a.m. — Continue tinkering with my query letter. I got some critiques back on it so I make some edits. I struggle sometimes with critical feedback but I know this will make it stronger, so I’m proud of myself for how I’m handling it. I have lunch, food from home, at my usual time. I’m annoyed about various work things and not in the best mood.

5:06 p.m. — Clock out and head home. Really glad to be off. Eat a random Unreal almond joy in my bag to tide me over until we make dinner later. When C. gets home, we go pick up the groceries (shrimp, tortillas, bread, seaweed, strawberries, jalapeño poppers, pork loin, avocados, lemons, cube cheese, string cheese, ground beef, broccoli, carrots, lemons, GF spaghetti noodles, oatmeal, potatoes — paid for yesterday). When we get there, I find out that they didn’t have shrimp or pork loin and never emailed me to let me know or try to substitute. ($14.73 back on the joint card). C. runs in and gets a lot of shrimp and a pork loin ($49.55 on the joint card). It’s so late by this point that we just give up and get Chipotle ($25.80 on the joint card). $30.31

7:15 p.m. — When we get home C. FaceTimes a friend while I get some writing done. I mostly tinker with my query letter (which is literally an endless task; it is never “finished”) and finish the second to last chapter. I just have one more chapter to go. C. says bye to their friend around 9:30 p.m. and we get in bed and fall asleep pretty quick.

Daily Total: $30.31

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Breakdown

Conclusion:
I think I did pretty decent this week. It was a somewhat average week, maybe on the lower end because typically we eat out more often, but we’ve been working on lessening that. The Pride event did give me the chance to spend some, and I did have to make some creative purchases, but overall I don’t think there’s much I would change. Keeping track of my spending actually made me feel better about what I’m buying and I feel more cognizant of the value I get from my purchases. In the future, I will probably have to be a bit more strict so I can pursue writing, but overall I think I’m not doing too bad.

title: Drawstring Pants Are Trending—Here’s How To Wear Them And The Best To Shop
text:
Drawstring Pants Are Trending—Here’s How To Wear Them And The Best To Shop

There’s something so undeniably cool about a comfortable outfit that manages to look incredibly chic at the same time. Right now, fashion lovers are anchoring those not-trying-too-hard looks with—the reason why we’re here—drawstring pants.

Yes, easy-to-pull-and-go, adjustable trousers are having quite the moment. In addition to spotting several ladies wearing them during Copenhagen Fashion Week, Google’s data shows that the search for them is increasing year over year. And what’s even better? They look much more sophisticated than any pair of leggings.

Wear them with a frilly lace blouse or an understated tank top, depending on your mood. What solidifies the look as an instant hit? Finishing touches, like a pendant necklace or statement sunnies.

My personal favorite aspect is that drawstring pants are breezy enough to wear on sweltering summer days yet they give you enough coverage for when temperatures start to change in the fall. Cost-per-wear is one of the most important aspects I consider when shopping, so anything that I can keep in rotation year-round always earns bonus points.

title: Rare Beauty’s New Fragrance Had Everyone Asking What I Was Wearing
text:
Rare Beauty’s New Fragrance Had Everyone Asking What I Was Wearing

When Selena Gomez released her inaugural fragrance for Rare Beauty, it quickly became one of my breakout favorite scents of 2025. Truthfully, I didn’t think she could outdo herself less than a year after such a successful first foray into the perfume world, but then she did just that earlier this month. Her sophomore scent, Rare Beginnings (which arguably makes a better name for a debut, but alas, I digress), is a departure from the dessert-like gourmand profile of Rare Eau de Parfum, breaking new ground in the world of fruity florals.

With notes of tart pear, sweet gardenia, and warm vanilla bean, Rare Beginnings sounded right up my alley on paper. (And it doesn’t hurt that the bottle is utterly gorgeous — a sage-green version of the original — not to mention an accessibility win, thanks to its wide, rounded top that’s easier to press.) I came of age in the 2000s and know my way around more than a few fruity scents; what I couldn’t have predicted, however, was just how much of a compliment magnet this would be. 

Rare Beginnings Eau de Parfum, $78

My first impression of Rare Beginnings was that it immediately reminded me of a grown-up version of Victoria’s Secret PINK body sprays (the ones in those rectangular-prism-shaped bottles). It has the same flirty, juicy sweetness of my beloved teenage splashes, but with the undertones of “she has a 401(k).” And speaking of grown-up, I’m calling it now: This is a great option for the office (or, if you’re controversial, the gym), since it’s light and fresh. When I hugged a friend at a recent happy hour, she told me I smelled amazing. Night made!

The OG Rare perfume also launched with a set of fragrance-layering balms designed to melt into the skin with body heat and enhance certain notes when layered under the perfume. With the arrival of Rare Beginnings, two more balms have joined the lineup: Fruity Pear and Sweet Marshmallow. 

At $78 for the full-size bottle (and $30 for the travel spray — the same as the original Rare), this is an expensive, gorgeous fruity scent that’s also something of a shapeshifter. When peared with the Fruity Pear balm, which smells delicious on its own, the succulent notes of pear nectar and lotus blossom really shine. With Sweet Marshmallow, which has a creamy, almost powdered-sugar-like quality, I found that the sneaky gourmand notes — candied pink sugar, nutty pistachio, and cozy vanilla bean — really come alive. In terms of longevity, I found that this one doesn’t linger quite as long as Rare, but I wasn’t totally surprised: Fruity notes tend to pull a disappearing act within a few hours of application, but I did find that Rare Beginnings tended to cling onto clothes much better than skin. 

Ultimately, I’d say lightning has struck twice with Rare Beginnings. Like its predecessor, it has a sweet, nostalgic quality, but with the polish of a proper eau de parfum — and, best of all, it works just as well at the office as it does on date night without missing a beat. Add in the layering balms for a little fragrance versatility, and you’ve got the beginning of your newest signature scent era.
