title: We Grew Up With Hayden Panettiere. Now We’re Reckoning With How Hollywood Failed Her.
text:
We Grew Up With Hayden Panettiere. Now We’re Reckoning With How Hollywood Failed Her.

On August 7, I turned 34. Birthdays have always made me reflective. During my new season, I take some time to think about where I am, where I thought I would be, what I’ve accomplished, what I still want, and how much of my childhood continues to influence the woman I’ve become. This year, though, turning 34 felt different. For the first time, I found myself really sitting with the fact that I am firmly in my mid-thirties, old enough to look backward with perspective and forward with a different understanding of time.  

Then, nine days later, I woke up with a strange pang in my chest. I checked my phone and learned that Hayden Panettiere, one of my favorite child actresses and a driving force across film and television throughout the 2000s, had died at 36. Details are still emerging but early reports say that Panettiere passed away from cardiac arrest, possibly due to an overdose, and that there was no evidence of foul play. She was only two years older than me, and for a moment, I couldn’t process it.  

Panettiere wasn’t simply an actress I admired. She was part of my childhood. Like so many millennial girls who grew up in the late 1990s and early 2000s, I watched her grow up on screen. I knew her from Remember the Titans, Ice Princess, Raising Helen, Bring It On: All or Nothing, Heroes and, later, Nashville. She was one of those young actors who seemed always to be there as we moved from childhood into adolescence and, eventually, adulthood. So, when the news of her death spread, it didn’t feel like the death of a celebrity I’d never met; it felt like the loss of someone I knew, like a childhood friend I’d lost touch with. I opened TikTok and watched montage after montage of the Golden Globe-nominated actress and mother, her death leaving most TikTokers in disbelief.   

Panettiere was only 36; we grew up with her, and she was so young. This doesn’t feel real. Between pouring over those TikToks, I realized that my grief wasn’t only about her. Panettiere’s life and now her death force my generation to confront the entertainment industry that raised us. Because millennials are old enough to remember these stars as children and now see them as adults, we’re seeing the aftereffects of growing up in the industry, and that perspective changes everything.  

We were too young to understand what it meant for a child to become a working actor. We saw the red carpets, the television shows, the magazine covers and the premieres. We saw talented young people seemingly living extraordinary lives. We didn’t see the pressure, the exploitation or the ways that childhood stardom could follow someone long after the cameras stopped rolling, and the pitfalls that come when the adults responsible for protecting them care more about money than their wellbeing.

And in Panettiere’s case, we didn’t understand how profoundly growing up inside Hollywood affected her until she began telling us herself. That’s when I started looking at child stardom differently. I remember growing up in the late 1990s and early 2000s surrounded by a generous array of “kid-friendly” entertainment programming. Nickelodeon’s All That, Disney’s That’s So Raven, Glee, made-for-television movies like Life-Size, and so much more filled our screens. These programs gave us characters we loved, actors we admired, and stories that became part of the fabric of our childhoods.  

But many of the young performers who helped create that cultural landscape never got the chance to grow old alongside us.   

Some passed away before they made it to their 40th birthdays (Cory Monteith died from an accidental heroin overdose at 31). Others have openly navigated addiction (Lindsay Lohan has been open about her struggles with substance abuse), mental illness (Amanda Bynes’ mental health battles have been highly publicized), and the difficult realities of transitioning from childhood fame into adulthood.  

That realization has become part of a larger millennial reckoning. Many of the child stars we grew up watching are no longer with us, like Michelle Trachtenberg, Brittany Murphy, Lee Thompson Young, and Aaron Carter. Their stories are not interchangeable, and Hollywood cannot be blamed for every tragedy. But collectively, they raise an uncomfortable question: What responsibility did the adults and institutions around these children have to protect them — and why did they so often fail?  

In Panettiere’s case, the answer can be found in what she revealed about her childhood. In her memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning, Panettiere wrote that she was introduced to drugs at 15 when a member of her public relations team allegedly gave her “happy pills” before red carpets and interviews to keep her focused and energetic. In a recent interview on the On Purpose with Jay Shetty podcast and in her memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning, Panettiere revealed how, at 19, she finally confronted her mother, Lesley Vogel, about their complicated relationship. While filming Heroes, Panettiere summoned the courage to end their professional relationship, telling her mother in her trailer during lunch, “I don’t want us to work together anymore. I just want you to be my mom.” Vogel cared more about the business than their relationship and told Panettiere that she “owed” her. Panettiere clearly didn’t receive the emotional support that a child is owed from her mother.

Panettiere also described the intense pressures of being raised in Hollywood from infancy and being managed and conditioned from a young age. That conditioning extended to encounters with powerful adults. Panettiere recalled in her memoir that an “important executive at NBC” kissed her on the lips at a party in 2008 while she was starring on Heroes. She also described an encounter at 19 in which an “Oscar-winning actor and director” allegedly cornered her and exposed himself.  

One of the most disturbing incidents occurred when she was 18. According to Panettiere and her memoir, an actress friend took her to a yacht party in the South of France and ushered her into a cabin where a famous British singer-songwriter in his 30s lay naked in bed.  

“I want you to get in bed with him,” the friend told her. Panettiere wrote that she panicked but had spent her life trusting the people managing her. “Being ‘managed’ was routine, to the point where I lost faith in my intuition,” she wrote.  

Her account speaks to something larger than one disturbing encounter: for the sake of our entertainment, these children sacrificed their freedom, lost trust in their own instincts, and fell victim to opportunistic, preying adults. When children become commodities, who is responsible for protecting them from a system built to profit from them? Panettiere later spoke openly about addiction to opioids and alcohol and her battle with postpartum depression. In a 2022 PEOPLE interview, she said, “I was on top of the world, and I ruined it.”  

That framing deserves reconsideration. Panettiere didn’t “ruin” her life; she was a young woman trying to survive circumstances she had been taught to normalize. She had to navigate fame and a relentless industry with no support or supervision. The only thing ruined was the sanctity, safety, and innocence of her childhood, which everyone has a right to.  

What’s most heartbreaking is that recently, it seemed as if Panettiere was finally entering a new chapter. On the On Purpose with Jay Shetty podcast, Panettiere said, “I finally feel like I have shaken off all of this darkness and this negativity.”  

That makes her death even more devastating. She was rebuilding and reclaiming her story, while bravely speaking openly about what had happened to her. And now, she is gone. We cannot know whether different interventions would have changed the course of Panettiere’s life. Her story was complicated, and it would be reductive to suggest Hollywood alone caused everything she endured.  

But we can acknowledge what the industry asked of Hayden Panettiere. It asked a child to become a professional before she was old enough to understand the power dynamics surrounding her. It asked her to perform, remain marketable and, at times, suppress her own instincts in service of a career adults were building around her.  

And when that child became an adult struggling with the consequences, the conversation too often became about what was wrong with her.  

In 2015, Panettiere openly spoke about her postpartum depression (PPD) and mental health struggles after giving birth to her daughter in 2014. That same year, she was dropped by cosmetics company Neutrogena after a 10-year partnership, a decision she believes was connected to her decision to speak publicly about her postpartum depression. Years later, in 2018, she made the painful decision to sign over full custody of her daughter to her then-partner, Wladimir Klitschko, so she could focus on recovering from severe postpartum depression and addiction. 

“I wouldn’t take [speaking about PPD] back, but…of all the things that I had been caught doing, that being the thing where they drew the line was shocking to me,” Panettiere told Shetty. She added that it was “heartbreaking” that their 10-year partnership ended without anyone from the company reaching out to her. 

Her problems became plotlines on Nashville. That is the part millennials should reckon with. We grew up consuming these stars’ childhoods without understanding the machinery behind them. Now we are old enough to look back and ask whether the adults were protecting the children — or protecting the machine.  

When I turned 34 this year, I found myself thinking about time differently, how childhood moves quickly into adulthood, what I want in this next chapter, and about the people I grew up watching. But Panettiere didn’t get to see 37. Her story allows us to reconsider what we owe the next generation of young performers. A child should not have to become the breadwinner before the adults around them decide to protect them. And even then, the money often still doesn’t buy them the love, security, and support they deserve.  

Millennials grew up watching Hayden Panettiere become a star, and unfortunately, now we are watching what that stardom cost her. Her struggles shouldn’t be the end of her story. Instead, her legacy should start a harder conversation about what Hollywood owes the children it turns into stars, and whether we are finally ready to demand better.

title: Drunk Elephant Finally Launched A Foundation — Sort Of
text:
Drunk Elephant Finally Launched A Foundation — Sort Of

Before Sephora tweens were even born, Drunk Elephant had already made a name for itself with buzzy skincare formulas that inspire fervent fanbases. And after more than a decade (and one $845 million acquisition deal later), the brand is finally giving its community a bucket-list product: foundation. (Sort of — more on that later.)

Drunk Elephant isn’t exactly a stranger to the makeup-skincare hybrid category. The brand’s viral bronzing drops (along with the lesser-known B-Goldi highlighting drops, which I actually prefer, not to mention O-Bloos Blush Drops) helped usher the concept of cocktailing complexion products into the mainstream, so it was only a matter of time before tinted complexion drops entered the chat. Meet Kamo Triple-Peptide Cover Drops.

“Kamo is a natural extension, perhaps evolution even, of our color drop family,” Drunk Elephant founder Tiffany Masterson says of the launch. Like its predecessors, it’s designed to be used in myriad ways: worn alone for the most comprehensive coverage, mixed with moisturizer for a sheer, skin-tint-like result, or combined into liquid illuminators (like Rhode’s Highlight Milk, for example) for a glowy finish.

In addition to a 4% concentration of skin barrier-supporting peptides, Kamo (available in 25 shades and retailing for $42) is infused with marula and green tea seed oils and squalane to moisturize skin and provide antioxidant benefits against pollution and UV damage. Ahead, three Refinery29 editors put the innovative drops to the ultimate summer wear test. 

Drunk Elephant Kamo Triple-Peptide Cover Drops, $42

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: Fair 4N 

“Makeup alchemy isn’t usually my thing. Rather than mix my products to perfection, I prefer to use a dedicated foundation or concealer as a base, but lately, nothing has been sitting right on my skin. It’s a combination of the unprecedented heat in London and using tretinoin (don’t worry, I’m diligent with sunscreen!), which has left me with flaky patches and uneven texture. With that in mind, I’ve been wearing more moisturizer, and the fact that I can mix these drops with my go-to (currently Prequel Half & Half Fluid Moisturizer — I love the ceramides!) has been a godsend in the soaring temperatures. 

I mix one drop (trust me, that’s all you need!) of Kamo into the milky lotion on the back of my hand, dunk my brush in — or what Katie Jane Hughes likes to call “priming” the brush — and apply all over. A single drop is enough to blanket breakouts and post-pimple staining. It’s even high-coverage enough that I can comfortably skip concealer under my eyes. It provides excellent coverage with a barely-there feel, but because one drop packs so much pigment, it really sticks around. I top mine off with setting spray, and I’m good to go from 8 a.m. until I come home in the evening.” — Jacqueline Kilikita, Beauty Director

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: 11N, 12W, 12N

“I love light, customizable coverage, so the concept of tailoring my complexion product was right up my alley. I liked being able to mix it into my day cream of choice (but never sunscreen, as this can disrupt the integrity of each formula, resulting in lower SPF protection than advertised) to create my own tinted moisturizer. A one-to-two ratio yielded a skin tint-like finish, while equal parts basically mimicked a medium-coverage foundation. 

My preferred method, however, ended up being really similar to our Beauty Director; after applying a tinted sunscreen (my go-to is EltaMD’s UV Clear in Medium), I dispensed a pump of Kamo (and as she mentioned, a little truly does go a very long way with this stuff), worked it into the bristles of a fluffy, medium-sized brush, and “airbrushed” any imperfections away. This resulted in glowy, hydrated skin that looked even, but not like I was wearing a makeup mask. Just for curiosity’s sake, I also tried wearing Kamo alone (which required about two pumps for my entire face), but that ended up looking a bit heavier than I like. That said, I’m not mad that it’s almost too concentrated; even with a relatively small bottle, I doubt I’ll finish it anytime soon.” —Karina Hoshikawa, Senior Beauty Writer 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Shade(s) tested: 23C, 25C, and 24N 

“Matching shades turned out to be an adventure. The Drunk Elephant team sent over 23C, 25C, and 24N after I let them know I fall into the rich category, but I probably should have been a bit more specific to land my exact match. I usually lean toward neutral undertones like 24N, but with a deep summer tan, I debated between 24N and 25C. When testing, I started with 23C on the back of my hand expecting a lighter swatch, but the color payoff has way more richness and depth once dispensed than it appears in the bottle.  

Even though 23C was deeper than my natural tone, just one drop blended out seamlessly across the outer areas of my face for a sheer, sculpted, bronze finish. Trying 24N proved even deeper, so 23C ended up being the sweet spot. The formula itself feels less like a traditional foundation and more like blending a weightless, nourishing serum into the skin.

I wish I had 22N in my arsenal (I think that would be my true perfect match), but either way, the ultra-blendable formula melted seamlessly into my skin. With just a light layer, it evens out hyperpigmentation while leaving my skin looking like, well, skin. Not caked-up or heavy at all. This is strictly for the girlies who want an effortless, no-makeup makeup look. I gave it a test drive on Sunday before church, and a woman on the elevator stopped me just to compliment how fresh-faced I looked. Honestly, those are the absolute best compliments.” — Alexis Bennett Parker, Director of Shopping Partnerships

title: JoJo On The Scents That Shaped Her Life, From Her Debut Album To Aquamarine
text:
JoJo On The Scents That Shaped Her Life, From Her Debut Album To Aquamarine

JoJo remembers her rise to fame with remarkable clarity — particularly the ferry ride into New Jersey to record her self-titled debut album, JoJo — because of how it smelled. A brand-new CD case. The papery scent of album liner notes. The warm, aromatic pull of the sandwich shop across the street from the studio. Those memories are embedded in her, as permanent as a signature scent.

“I was bullied in school because I was always very eccentric,” she says, recalling belting out Christina Aguilera songs on the jungle gym as a kid. “When Christina came out with her fragrance, it was such a concept to me — that maybe if I wore her fragrance, I could sound like her. Maybe I could turn into her,” JoJo recalls.

Not long afterwards, she burst onto the scene with her debut single, “Leave (Get Out),” becoming the youngest solo artist ever to top the Billboard Pop Songs chart at just 13 years old. What followed was a string of hits — “Too Little Too Late”, “Baby It’s You” and “Say So” — as well as a starring role alongside Emma Roberts and Sara Paxton in the 2006 teen fantasy movie Aquamarine. “That was such a moment,” she says. “All of us girls were inspiring each other and sharing beauty products like lotions and sunscreen and just looking out for each other.”

If she had to bottle that chapter of her life today? It would smell like EOS Beach Waves 24H Moisture Body Lotion & Body Mist and Toasted Marshmallow 24H Moisture Body Lotion & Body Mist. Equal parts tropical, sweet, and comforting. But what does the future smell like to JoJo? “Let’s see,” she muses. “The next 12 months smells like ascension. It smells like expansion. Jazz. Golden hour. New York City. Europe.”

Listen to the full podcast episode, where JoJo joins Nose Dive host Asia Grant — an NYC-based independent perfumer and creative director — for a conversation about opening for Usher, making her first album, her favorite celebrity fragrances of the ’00s, channeling confidence through scent, and so much more.
